papers.title: FE DEFICIENCY-INDUCED KELCH REPEAT PROTEIN 1 (FDK1) links coumarin metabolism and iron homeostasis during alkaline iron deficiency in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Although iron (Fe) is abundant in soils, its low solubility, particularly under alkaline conditions, often limits plant Fe acquisition. Under these conditions, coumarin-mediated Fe mobilization becomes increasingly important. Arabidopsis thaliana FE DEFICIENCY-INDUCED KELCH REPEAT PROTEIN 1 (FDK1, AT3G07720) is strongly induced by Fe deficiency and regulated by the central transcription factor FIT, but its function is unknown. We investigated FDK1 using genetic, physiological, metabolite, and transcriptomic analyses. Loss of FDK1 altered root growth, whereas this phenotype was restored in the FDK1-Ox overexpression line. Under alkaline Fe deficiency, growth medium from FDK1-Ox contained strongly increased levels of the Fe-mobilizing coumarins fraxetin and esculetin compared with wild type, whereas their induction was attenuated in fdk1-1. RNA-seq analysis linked FDK1 abundance to coumarin biosynthesis and iron-homeostasis gene expression. FIT and many FIT-associated genes were highly expressed in FDK1-Ox, whereas several upstream iron-homeostasis regulators, including bHLH Ib factors, were highest in fdk1-1. These findings identify FDK1 as a component of the alkaline Fe-deficiency response that promotes iron-mobilizing coumarin accumulation and is associated with coordinated regulation of iron-homeostasis genes.

papers.title: The Red Blood Cell Surface Defines a Distinct Tumor DNA Compartment for Liquid Biopsy
papers.abstract: Red blood cells (RBCs) modulate host inflammatory responses by scavenging mitochondrial and pathogen DNA. However, how RBC surface properties govern the capture of tumor-derived DNA remains poorly understood. We show that RBCs tether and retain tumor-derived DNA on their surface, forming a distinct circulating pool of RBC-bound tumor DNA (rtDNA). Desialylation increased DNA capture in a Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)-dependent manner, identifying RBC surface sialylation and TLR9 as a regulator of DNA binding. In mice bearing lung cancer xenografts, rtDNA was detected in all animals and its abundance correlated with tumor burden, whereas tumor DNA was undetectable in matched plasma samples. In patients with lung cancer, the majority of detected mutant tumor DNA was associated with RBCs rather than plasma, and RBC-derived mutations were concordant with molecular alterations identified in matched tumor tissue. Collectively, these findings establish the RBC surface as a tunable site of tumor-DNA capture and retention and challenge the plasma-centric paradigm of liquid biopsy by identifying a distinct cellular reservoir of tumor-derived genetic material.

papers.title: scPRIME-seq uncovers synchronized multimodal molecular collapse facilitated by pre-neoplastic epigenetic burden in prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Tumorigenesis involves alterations across the genome, epigenome and transcriptome, yet how these layers interact to drive malignant transformation remains unclear, largely due to the lack of scalable multimodal single-cell approaches. Here, we developed scPRIME-seq, a high-throughput platform for simultaneous single-cell profiling of transcriptome, genome and DNA methylome, and applied it to 436,908 cells from 29 prostate cancers and 15 benign tissues. This multimodal atlas resolved dynamic changes across 30 cell types and a unified tumorigenic trajectory. Integrated analysis revealed a cell-state transition tipping point, where the onset of aneuploidy is temporally coupled with global methylomic alterations and transcriptomic rewiring. Early focal epigenetic alterations, including TMEM106A promoter hypermethylation and the emergence of hypomethylated domains, were present in founder aneuploid clones and benign tissues, indicating a pre-neoplastic origin of epigenetic burden. These pre-neoplastic alterations coincide with transcriptomic changes that affect epithelial interactions with stromal and immune compartments, promoting a putative tumor-permissive microenvironment. scPRIME-seq provides a high-throughput multimodal framework for identifying conserved, cell-intrinsic molecular programs underlying tumorigenesis.

papers.title: Loss of the Y chromosome is transcriptionally silent in clear cell renal cell carcinoma and across cancer entities
papers.abstract: Tumors in men often lose the Y chromosome. In some tumor types, this is predictive of poor outcome. Given the male predominance and high LOY frequency in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), we asked whether LOY might impact the transcriptome of ccRCC. We determined somatic Y chromosome status and performed differential expression analysis on tumor RNA-sequencing samples of two human ccRCC cohorts (TCGA-KIRC, CPTAC-ccRCC) and in an autochthonous murine ccRCC model with renal epithelium-specific deletion of Vhl, Trp53 and Rb1. We additionally derived five isogenic Y-deficient and five Y chromosome-retaining clones of the human ccRCC cell line 786-O. Across all three settings, transcriptional changes were largely restricted to the expected gene dosage effects of male-specific Y (MSY) and pseudoautosomal region (PAR) genes, without large effects on autosomal genes. At the pathway level, we identified a modest but reproducible response in the human cohorts, converging on cell cycle, ribosomal biogenesis and DNA repair genes. A pan-cancer meta-analysis across TCGA entities recovered the same pattern, with no autosomal gene showing a large consistent effect. In some entities, but not in ccRCC, cancer/testis antigen expression was higher in LOY tumors. We conclude that, apart from direct gene dosage, modest pathway-level shifts and altered silencing of cancer/testis antigens, LOY is transcriptionally silent in adult humans and mice. Y-chromosomal genes are therefore unlikely to act as transcriptional drivers of ccRCC and other cancer entities.

papers.title: An Immunocompetent Mouse Model of Degarelix Induced Chemical Castration to Investigate Acquired Resistance to Androgen Deprivation.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer (PC) remains a significant health concern as the second leading cause of cancer-related death in American men. Androgen deprivation therapies represent the standard of care for patients with PC, regardless of disease stage. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists, such as Degarelix, are commonly used hormone therapies for PC and work by suppressing testosterone production. Previous studies indicate a prostate involution-regeneration cycle following surgical castration and testosterone addback. However, whether a similar response occurs following pharmacologic androgen deprivation with agents such as Degarelix remains poorly understood. In particular, the temporal dynamics of prostate involution and subsequent regeneration after chemical castration have not been systematically defined. Our study utilizes immunocompetent mouse models to evaluate the systemic and temporal effects of Degarelix treatment and determine its efficacy in suppressing PC tumor growth. We show that continuous Degarelix treatment significantly suppressed systemic testosterone levels in mice, whereas testosterone levels returned to physiological baseline following Degarelix withdrawal. Gross anatomical, H&E, and Trichrome analyses demonstrated that Degarelix induced castration resulted in prostate involution, characterized by reduced gland size and increased stromal remodeling. This phenotype was reversed after Degarelix withdrawal, highlighting the reversibility of pharmacological androgen deprivation. Immunofluorescence staining revealed changes in basal and luminal epithelial cell populations within the prostatic gland, indicating changes in prostate glandular architecture following Degarelix induced castration and subsequent regeneration. Next, we evaluated the impact of chemical castration on PC tumor growth. Although Degarelix initially suppressed tumor growth, this response was not sustained through the study endpoint, suggesting the emergence of acquired resistance to androgen deprivation. These findings establish this immunocompetent model as a physiologically relevant platform for dissecting the mechanisms that drive therapeutic resistance and tumor progression following androgen deprivation. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of chemical castration with Degarelix and establish a robust model to study both therapeutic responses and the emergence of castration resistance in PC.

papers.title: Targeting ribosome biogenesis sensitizes PARPi-resistant triple-negative breast cancer
papers.abstract: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) are the only targeted treatment available for early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), an aggressive subtype with limited treatment options. While PARPi are effective in patients with BRCA mutations, resistance to these inhibitors can arise. We previously developed BRCA-mutant cell lines, HCC1395, with acquired resistance to talazoparib and olaparib, and have now developed PARPi-resistant MX1 cell lines in an analogous manner. Ribosomal pathways were upregulated in 3/4 cell lines with acquired PARPi resistance. The resistant cell lines showed high and low basal nucleolar stress based on nucleolar morphology and nucleophosmin delocalization from nucleolus to nucleoplasm. Treatment of these cell lines with the combination of olaparib and a ribosome biogenesis inhibitor, BMH-21, demonstrated synergy in the PARPi-resistant cell lines, but not in the parental cells. Interestingly, HCC1395 cells, which had lower baseline nucleolar stress, showed greater nucleophosmin delocalization with combination treatment than MX1 cells, which had higher baseline nucleolar stress. All four cell lines demonstrated sustained DNA damage with the combination. We extended our investigation to 3 BRCA wild-type TNBC cell lines, BT549, Hs578T, and MDAMB231 and identified synergy in the context of intrinsic PARPi resistance. In MDAMB231 cells, combining olaparib with BMH-21 induced a senescence-like phenotype, increasing gH2AX-positive cells by up to 7.3-fold, senescence-associated B-galactosidase (SA-B-gal) staining by 5.6-fold, and p21 by 3.6-fold. These results were mirrored with a second ribosome biogenesis inhibitor, CX-5461. Finally, we identified distinct patterns of ribosomal pathway activity in a cohort of patients with treatment-resistant TNBC, and found correlations between ribosomal pathways with MYC, proliferation, DNA damage, and senescence. Together, these data identify ribosome biogenesis as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in PARPi-resistant TNBC and support its targeting in combination with PARPi, while demonstrating a broader for ribosome biogenesis in treatment-resistant TNBC.

papers.title: Bacterial dispersal and host specificity shape microbiome strain sharing among great ape species in neighboring zoo exhibits
papers.abstract: Animal microbiomes often exhibit host-species-specific structure, which could suggest a shared evolutionary history with their hosts. However, in wild populations this possibility has been difficult to disentangle from geographic or ecological barriers to microbial dispersal, particularly in taxa like non-human primates in which phylogeny and geography are closely related. To investigate microbiome transmission and adaptation in a common environment, the gut microbiomes of zoo-housed great apes were profiled longitudinally for four months. Even in a shared environment, phylogenetic structure emerged in both species- and strain-level microbiome composition. Longitudinal tracking of new strain acquisitions revealed that transmission across exhibits was possible, even between distantly related host species, suggesting that phylogenetic structure emerged in the longer term as different strains survived in different hosts. Comparison to metagenomes from humans and wild great apes revealed little evidence that human keepers, researchers, or zoo guests drive transmission between exhibits. Instead, across-exhibit transmission disproportionately involved spore-forming bacterial genera, possibly suggesting airborne spore transmission as a means of bacterial dispersal. By investigating microbiomes of different host species in a common geographic environment without direct inter-host interaction, this study identifies spatial constraints on transmission, bacterial dispersal ability, and differential survival of bacterial strains in different hosts as factors shaping the gut microbiomes of great apes.

papers.title: Heritable variation in root bacterial microbiomes alters natural selection on host plants
papers.abstract: Heritable variation in microbiome composition could theoretically evolve in response to selection acting on hosts, but empirical evidence of this is scarce. We tested for effects of allelic variation in Boechera stricta on microbiome composition and downstream consequences for host fitness. In the greenhouse, near-isogenic lines with contrasting phytochemistry alleles differentially conditioned soil microbiota in ways that changed the relative fecundity of host genotypes. In the field, root microbiome differences mediated allelic effects on host fitness. Selection gradients on individual taxa and multivariate axes of root microbiome composition suggest that independent components of the bacterial community favor each allele, especially under drought. These results show that microbiota contribute to natural selection on a major-effect phytochemistry gene, empirically closing the loop between microbiome heritability and host trait evolution.

papers.title: A gut-on-chip model reveals architecture-dependent epithelial responses to microbial challenge
papers.abstract: Advanced in vitro models that better recapitulate human intestinal physiology are needed to improve translational relevance and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. Microfluidic gut-on-chip systems provide controlled architectural and mechanical microenvironments that more closely resemble native tissue than conventional static cultures. However, how these features influence epithelial responses to microbial stimuli remains incompletely understood. In this study, we compared conventional two-dimensional (2D) Caco-2 monolayers with a perfused three-dimensional (3D) gut-on-chip model exhibiting crypt-like epithelial organization. Microbial challenge was employed as a biologically relevant perturbation to investigate barrier-associated responses under distinct culture conditions. Following exposure to the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), epithelial morphology, barrier-associated gene expression, inflammatory signaling, and temporal response patterns were assessed over time. In a complementary approach, susceptibility to bacterial stress was examined using increasing doses of Citrobacter rodentium (C. rodentium). Both culture systems responded dynamically to microbial exposure; however, differences in response patterns were observed between static and perfused cultures. EcN induced transient alterations in epithelial organization followed by recovery-associated responses, while C. rodentium caused dose-dependent structural and transcriptional changes. Notably, epithelial damage became apparent at lower bacterial loads in conventional 2D cultures, whereas the chip-based model maintained tissue integrity under comparable conditions. Together, these findings indicate that epithelial architecture and the surrounding culture environment influence barrier-associated responses to microbial challenge. The study highlights the utility of gut-on-chip systems for investigating host-microbe interactions and provides a framework for functional comparison of advanced intestinal in vitro models.

papers.title: Mouse oocytes organize mRNA-protein assemblies and ER-associated translation hubs to drive meiosis
papers.abstract: Oocyte meiosis in animals is essential for producing fertilizable eggs. As transcription becomes largely quiescent, meiotic progression depends on temporally regulated translation of accumulated maternal mRNAs. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identified diverse and highly organized mRNA-protein assemblies in mouse oocytes that coordinate cytoplasmic mRNA regulation and enable spatiotemporal translation to drive oocyte meiosis. Twelve RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), including DDX4/VASA, HDLBP/Vigilin, and TDRD3, were assembled into widely distributed aggregates in germinal vesicle (GV)-stage oocytes. We depleted DDX4 and HDLBP using Trim-Away and found that these RBPs regulate the precise assembly of RNA granules and protein aggregates through distinct mechanisms, promoting temporal protein synthesis at cortical translation factories with the endoplasmic reticulum, termed CORTE. All 12 RBPs formed distinct mRNA-protein assemblies, whose size and distribution changed upon meiotic initiation. These findings reveal the molecular basis of spatiotemporal mRNA-protein-organelle networks underlying animal reproduction and development.

papers.title: Organelle Volume Facilitates Spindle Positioning During C. elegans Female Meiosis
papers.abstract: Cortical positioning of oocyte meiotic spindles is required for reducing chromosome number by segregating chromosomes into polar bodies. In C. elegans, kinesin-1 transports membrane-bound organelles inward into a central ball that is hypothesized to push the meiotic spindle outward. Using focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy, we found that the percent volume occupied by membrane-bound organelles was 28% in a mature oocyte that has completed endocytosis of the yolk precursor, vitellogenin, compared to 17% in a less mature oocyte that has not yet endocytosed vitellogenin. We therefore hypothesized that blocking endocytosis of vitellogenin would reduce the size of the central ball of organelles packed inward by kinesin-1 and limit outward movement of the spindle. Depletion of vitellogenin or proteins required for endocytosis resulted in a smaller central volume of kinesin-coated organelles and defective spindle positioning. A computer simulation of a simple exclusion model faithfully recapitulated wildtype and mutant spindle position phenotypes. These results support a volume exclusion model for positioning acentriolar meiotic spindles.

papers.title: Calpain-mediated regulation of WAVE tyrosine dephosphorylation by PTP61F promotes lamellipodia formation
papers.abstract: WAVE is a major driver of lamellipodial protrusions. Previous studies suggested that Abelson (Abl)-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of WAVE promotes actin polymerization and lamellipodia formation. Here, we provide evidence that Abl tyrosine kinase rather restricts lamellipodial localization of WAVE and inhibits lamellipodial cell spreading. Additionally, overexpression of a cytoplasmic PTP61F phosphatase increases WAVE localization at lamellipodia tips. PTP61F overexpression or pharmacological inhibition of Abl/Src kinases even protects cells from lamellipodia disruption induced by pervanadate, a potent protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor. By contrast, overexpression of a phosphatase-deficient PTP61F trapping mutant phenocopies loss of wave function. We identify the tyrosine Y234 as a prominent phosphorylation site in WAVE. Rescue experiments using CRISPR/Cas9-based KO wave mutant cells confirmed an important role of PTP61F-mediated WAVE dephosphorylation in lamellipodia formation. Our data suggest a model in which calpain-mediated proteolytic release of ER-bound PTP61F antagonizes Abl/Src-dependent WAVE phosphorylation and acts as a mechanism promoting re-localization of WAVE to lamellipodial tips.

papers.title: Cell-specific FUS loss enhances ageing-associated transcriptional elongation in lung fibrosis
papers.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is an age-related, lethal lung disease affecting over 3 million people worldwide. During aging, impairment of diverse molecular processes compromises cellular homeostasis. Eukaryotic cells adapt to this ageing-associated stress by large-scale transcriptome changes affecting the expression of genes involved in signaling, protein homeostasis, cell plasticity and immune response. The molecular mechanisms regulating extensive transcriptome rearrangements leading to senescence in specific cell types of IPF lungs remain sparsely investigated. Here we uncover fundamental molecular mechanisms underlying cellular senescence by integrative analysis of multi-omics studies and functional experiments monitoring fibrotic and senescence hallmarks in primary lung fibroblasts from control and IPF patients. Loss-of-function of the DNA/RNA binding protein fused in sarcoma (FUS) in control fibroblasts enhanced fibrotic and senescence hallmarks resembling IPF fibroblasts. Dissecting the molecular mechanisms, reduced FUS levels in IPF fibroblasts abolished R-loop formation at transcription start sites (TSS), leading to increased RNA polymerase II (Pol II) recruitment and its phosphorylation at serine 2, resulting in enhanced translocation speed of elongating Pol II and increased expression of fibrosis- and senescence-related genes. Summarizing, FUS maintains low Pol II processivity in control fibroblasts by stabilizing R-loops at TSS, acting as a gatekeeper of fibrotic and age-associated transcriptional programs.

papers.title: MDS-causing mutations of ZRSR2 impair minor intron splicing by reducing its interaction with SF3B complex
papers.abstract: Minor introns are rare but evolutionarily conserved introns in the human genome. Defects in minor spliceosome components have been reported to cause several human diseases. Mutations in ZRSR2 are frequently observed in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) patients. However, the precise molecular mechanism by which these mutations cause a loss of ZRSR2 function in minor intron splicing remain elusive. In this study, we characterized the impact of MDS-causing missense mutations in ZRSR2. Most of the mutant ZRSR2 proteins we tested showed different subnuclear localization pattern from that of wild-type ZRSR2 protein. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) analysis revealed that UHM missense mutations disrupted the interaction between ZRSR2 and SF3B complex. We also demonstrated that ZRSR2 preferentially immunoprecipitated minor spliceosome components over major spliceosome components and it directly interacts with SF3B1. Furthermore, co-IP analysis utilizing a variety of ZRSR2 mutants revealed that mutations in the UHM and Zn2 domains significantly attenuated the interaction with SF3B complex. Finally, UHM and Zn2 mutations markedly disrupted the supporting activity of ZRSR2 for minor intron splicing. Our results indicate that disruption of the physical interaction with SF3B complex is one of the hallmarks of MDS-causing mutations of ZRSR2, which results in aberrant splicing of minor introns.

papers.title: Multi-domain analysis of the fecal microbiome of dairy heifers, beef heifers, bred beef heifers, and adult beef cows in the central United States using paired 16S rRNA and 18S rRNA metabarcoding
papers.abstract: The growth and performance of cattle is dependent on efficient feed conversion, facilitated by the gut microbiome, including both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. Extrinsic factors such as management practices and intrinsic factors like age and genetics can shape these communities. To characterize the relative effects of such factors on the prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbiomes, fresh fecal samples from dairy heifers (n = 8), beef heifers (n = 8), bred beef heifers (n = 8), and adult beef cows (n = 8) were subjected to paired 16S rRNA (V4) and a novel 18S rRNA (V4-V5) metabarcoding assay, and 18S rRNA amplicons were annotated using two databases in parallel. Taxonomic resolution of 18S rRNA amplicons was excellent, with SILVA and EUKARYOME databases each providing better resolution of different groups of organisms. While no differences in eukaryotic richness or alpha diversity were detected, beta diversity differed in all pairwise comparisons except between beef heifers and bred beef heifers. Prokaryotic richness was lower in adult beef cows than the other groups, and beta diversity differed in all pairwise comparisons. Adult beef cows were the most distinct, characterized by replacement of fungal organisms with protozoa and loss of thermophilic bacteria in the eukaryotic and prokaryotic compartments, respectively. Among numerous differentially abundant features, dairy heifers harbored greater abundance of Cooperia oncophora while beef heifers contained greater abundance of Buxtonella sulcata and Mucor. Correlation network analysis revealed multiple significant positive and negative associations between bacterial, fungal, and protozoal features during maturation of the fecal microbiome. Collectively, these data highlight the richness and diversity of both the prokaryotic and eukaryotic compartments of the bovine fecal microbiome, and the influence of management practices and age on both communities. From a technical standpoint, these data demonstrate the ability to resolve fungal, protozoal, and metazoan organisms, including potential parasites and pathogens, with a single metabarcoding assay. They also highlight the nuanced differences between databases and the value of parallel analyses using more than one database.

papers.title: Higher-Order Organization Links Circulating Metabolites to Glucocorticoid Action in Human Adipose Tissue
papers.abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) are regulators of metabolism, yet how physiological GC exposure remodels adipose metabolism and its relationship with circulating biomarkers remains poorly understood. In a randomised cross-over study of individuals with primary adrenal insufficiency, near-physiological GC exposure was compared to withdrawal using integrated serum metabolomics, abdominal subcutaneous microdialysis metabolomics, and adipose tissue transcriptomics. GC exposure induced coordinated changes in adipose lipid and amino-acid metabolism. Pathway-level entropy analysis revealed GC-state-dependent transcriptional reorganisation, with concentrated organisation during exposure and diffuse organisation during withdrawal. Integrative hypergraph and topological analyses revealed GC-state-dependent reorganisation of circulating metabolite-adipose tissue relationships, with greater higher-order coordination during exposure. The circulating phenylalanine/kynurenine ratio discriminated GC state, showed the strongest shared connectivity to GC-regulated adipose networks, persisted at midnight and in an independent dose-response study, and exhibited circadian rhythmicity. These findings reveal dynamic GC regulation of adipose metabolism and identify a circulating biomarker with potential to guide personalised GC therapy.

papers.title: Archetype analysis of multiplexed antibody imaging reveals interpretable morphological programs in optical pooled screens
papers.abstract: High-content imaging-based screens with small molecule or genetic perturbations rely on rich optical phenotypes, yet how distinct subcellular markers contribute complementary biological information remains unclear. Here, we introduce CellMAPP, a multiplexed organelle imaging platform that uses optical pooled screens with iterative antibody staining to map cellular architecture under perturbation. Using 17 markers across 524 genetic perturbations in MCF-7 cells, we systematically examined how individual, and combinations of, markers capture diverse morphological responses. We find that markers provide complementary views of perturbation effects, with increased multiplexing improving signal and the breadth of hit recovery, although some phenotypes are better recovered from a subset of features rather than a full profile. Because non-molecular image-based profiles can be challenging to link with interpretable biology, we developed CHART (available at https://github.com/Genentech/CHART), an archetype analysis framework that identifies distinct reference morphological states for each marker and uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to automatically annotate them, connecting cellular images to recognizable organelle phenotypes. Integrating archetypes across multiple markers revealed modular morphological programs that describe coordinated organelle reorganization in response to perturbation. This framework identified regulators of defined organelle states such as micronuclei, nominated novel gene functions and revealed complex patterns of multi-organelle reposition. Together, optical profiling with MAPP and CHART provides an interpretable, scalable framework for image-based screens that sheds light on rules governing cellular structural reprogramming.

papers.title: High-throughput in vivo DNA data encoding by multiplexed conjugationand orthogonal base editing
papers.abstract: Bacterial conjugation and CRISPR base editing offer complementary routes for programmable DNA transfer and heritable genomic writing, but their combined potential for information encoding in living cells remains unexplored. Here, we introduce CONCORD, a bacterial encoding platform that couples multiplexed bacterial conjugation to genomic base editing for synthesis-free in vivo DNA data writing. A recipient Writer strain expresses the base-editing machinery and is equipped with a writing template, whereas reusable donor Guide strains deliver the encoding sgRNA signals by conjugation. Using this setup, we encode binary information into genomic DNA in a high-throughput manner. Moreover, we systematically evaluated multiple orthogonal base editors for an expanded encoding repertoire and improved data recovery through redundancy encoding. We deploy the system to encode 45,689 bits into DNA including two culturally and historically significant artifacts: a greeting from NASA's Voyager Golden Record and a photograph of Navajo petroglyphs and recovered these datasets with 100% and 99.5% accuracy, respectively, without computational error correction. Connecting and engineering the unique mating and immune system of microbial cells we have established a framework for programmable information writing in bacterial populations, with applications for biological event recording and sustainable DNA data storage.

papers.title: Sense-and-response to intracellular signaling via nucleocytoplasmic localization control of a synthetic transcription factor platform
papers.abstract: Many therapeutically relevant signaling pathways are sensed inside the cell, yet a modular synthetic biology platform for responding to intracellular signaling at the post-translational level is lacking. Signaling pathways control the nuclear localization and activity of native transcription factors via phosphorylation of nuclear localization/export or cytoplasmic anchor sequences. Here, we apply this concept to develop a platform of nucleocytoplasmic localization tags (NCtags) that control the nuclear translocation of a synthetic transcription factor (synTF) for transgene induction in engineered cells. We identify human-based synTF components that are basally cytoplasmic and induce transgenes under the control of NCtags with minimal background. We demonstrate the modular nature of this platform through transcriptional reporter induction in response to a calcium-inducible NFAT-derived NCtag, and development of novel NCtags responsive to hyperosmolarity, cAMP, or logical combinations of cAMP and calcium. Multiple factors in the tumor microenvironment elevate cAMP in T cells, leading to reduced function. We demonstrate that NCtag-synTF fusions expressed in T cells can respond to endogenous sources of cAMP or calcium in breast cancer spheroids to induce transgene expression. Our use of human components and an all-in-one lentiviral vector encoding the NCtag-synTF-transgene system establishes this as a novel platform for sense-and-response inside therapeutic cells.

papers.title: Directed evolution of a thermostable family-A DNA polymerase into a reverse transcriptase for 2'-modified RNA
papers.abstract: RNA-based therapeutics increasingly rely on nuclease-resistant xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs), but engineering polymerases capable of reading and amplifying these non-canonical substrates remains a major challenge. Natural DNA polymerases cannot process C2' sugar modifications, and the complete structural determinants governing this limitation remain poorly understood, limiting rational design strategies. In this study, we apply directed evolution methods to Thermus thermophilus DNA polymerase using a microfluidic implementation of the Compartmentalized Self-Replication (CSR). We identify an engineered variant, termed E5, capable of reverse transcribing C2'-modified RNA, a previously inaccessible activity for this enzyme. Next-generation sequencing allow us to track evolutionary trajectories across nine rounds of evolution. Through an integrated analysis combining statistical methods, protein language models, and crystallographic data, we reveal unknown epistatic networks controlling polymerase function. This large-scale experimental dataset (>196,000 thermostable enzyme variants) provides a robust basis for predicting sequence-to-function relationships, accelerating development of enzymes for aptamer discovery and synthetic biology applications.

papers.title: VesiScope: A stand-alone tool for the automatic detection, quantification and size analysis of GUVs from phase contrast microscopy images
papers.abstract: Fluorescence microscopy is routinely used in the quantitative analysis of Giant Unilamellar Vesicles (GUVs) because it makes GUVs visible and easy to detect. Nonetheless, it requires fluorescence-equipped microscopes and, especially, the addition of tagged molecules that may introduce undesired and unaccounted variations compared to the pristine formulation. Alternatively, phase-contrast microscopy can be used to observe GUVs without labelling, yet the automatic detection of GUVs in phase-contrast images by standard image processing techniques is difficult. To overcome this limitation, we developed a framework for the automated detection and size characterization of label-free GUVs based on YOLOv11 model, a state-of-art lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for object detection. Trained on 164 phase-contrast microscope images containing 4666 manually annotated vesicles, the model enables robust detection under low contrast-to-noise ratio and heterogeneous illumination. The trained model is implemented in a stand-alone desktop application supporting multiple analysis in a single run, pixel-to-micrometer calibration, and automated size distribution analysis. This approach achieves high detection accuracy and competitive cross-microscope generalization using YOLOv11 nano on greyscale image. Retraining scripts compatible with standard hardware are also provided to enhance adaptability. This tool enables fast and reliable analysis of GUVs without altering their composition, supporting experimental reproducibility.

papers.title: User-friendly software for high-throughput processing of chlorophyll fluorescence images to assess plant stress responses: fvfmPy and fvfmR packages
papers.abstract: Chlorophyll fluorescence imaging is a powerful tool used to characterize abiotic and biotic stress response of photosynthesis in plants. However, extracting metrics such as Fv/Fm (maximum quantum yield of photosystem II) from chlorophyll fluorescence images remains a substantial bottleneck in large measurement campaigns, often requiring significant manual effort. To resolve this issue, we developed fvfmPy, a user-friendly program which enables rapid analysis of chlorophyll fluorescence images of arrays of leaf discs. fvfmPy uses algorithmic image segmentation to identify regions of interest and extract fluorescence metrics from tens or hundreds of leaf samples per image with little to no manual input. fvfmPy is developed in Python and includes a graphical user interface enabling intuitive parameter adjustment and real-time quality control checking. We additionally developed fvfmR, an R wrapper package for fvfmPy. Fv/Fm values extracted with fvfmPy were indistinguishable from those obtained using manual methods (r2 > 0.99) but required 94% less time to complete (13 s vs. 200 s per 100 measurements). fvfmPy and fvfmR were built to directly integrate with existing fluorescence software packages and can greatly increase throughput of fluorescence measurements to help address key challenges in agriculture and ecology.

papers.title: Genome-scale mapping of plant transcription factor effector domains reveals conserved regulatory principles across eukaryotes
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic life spans species that diverged over a billion years ago, yet our molecular view of gene regulation remains heavily skewed toward Opisthokonta model systems, particularly yeast and humans. The degree to which the protein features governing transcriptional regulation are conserved across eukaryotes or have diversified within individual eukaryotic supergroups remains unresolved. To provide a distinct evolutionary reference point, we used a massively parallel reporter assay in plant cells to identify transcriptional effector domains and define their sequence constraints, measuring ~26,000 protein fragments tiling nearly all Arabidopsis transcription factors (1,859 proteins). Comparison with the activity of the same peptide sequences in yeast revealed that activation is governed by a mixture of deeply conserved biochemical features and lineage-dependent functional differences across widely divergent eukaryotic lineages. Likewise, plant repression domains are governed by flexible sequence grammars that extend beyond conserved repression motifs. Together, these results reveal both broadly conserved and clade-specific principles governing eukaryotic transcriptional regulation.

papers.title: Hidden Medicines in Herbarium Collections: Medicinal Plant Diversity and Ethnopharmacological Knowledge from GSUH, Nigeria
papers.abstract: Herbarium collections represent an important but frequently underutilized source of information for documenting medicinal plant diversity and preserving ethnomedicinal knowledge. We assessed the medicinal plant diversity represented in herbarium records from the Gombe State University Herbarium (GSUH), Nigeria, and evaluated patterns in taxonomic composition, therapeutic applications, and plant parts reported for medicinal use. We also tested the hypothesis that the plant parts used medicinally are not randomly distributed across therapeutic or ailment categories, but that particular plant parts are disproportionately associated with specific therapeutic applications. The resulting dataset comprised 1,576 specimen records, including 768 recorded as medicinal plant species across 94 families and 1,426 medicinal-use records (Table S1). Fabaceae was the most species-rich family (15.8%), followed by Asteraceae (9.3%), Malvaceae (4.8%), Lamiaceae (4.4%), Rubiaceae (3.2%), and Apocynaceae (3.2%). The most frequently represented therapeutic themes were infections and sexually transmitted diseases (50.7%), gastrointestinal disorders (41.9%), pain, inflammation, and rheumatism (41.9%), fever and malaria (40.2%), and skin diseases and wounds (40.0%). Individual species had a mean of 2.98 therapeutic themes, with medicinal breadth ranging from 1 to 7 themes. A species-aware permutation test confirmed that the observed plant-part and therapeutic-theme association was significantly stronger than expected under random association (9,999 permutations, P < 0.0001). These findings demonstrate the value of herbarium collections as taxonomically anchored resources for recovering information on medicinal plant diversity. Integrating herbarium records with published ethnomedicinal knowledge provides a reproducible framework for linking plant diversity, taxonomy and traditional medicinal applications and highlights the potential of underutilised African herbaria for ethnopharmacological research.

papers.title: A Synergistic Terpenoid-Phenolic Defense Network Confers Resistance to Dendrolimus superans in Hybrid Larch
papers.abstract: To elucidate the resistance of hybrid larch (Larix spp.) clones to Dendrolimus superans and their chemical defense mechanisms, 46 clones were subjected to field feeding-infestation experiments. Insect resistance was comprehensively evaluated by the membership function method from three perspectives: insect weight change, frass weight and defoliation rate (damage consequences); pre- and post-infestation physiological indices (constitutive and induced resistance). High- and low-resistance materials screened from each perspective were further analyzed by widely targeted LC-MS metabolomics. The three damage indices differed highly significantly among clones (P 90%). The three groups yielded 1,010, 1,086 and 922 differentially accumulated metabolites, and PCA separated high- from low-resistance materials in all groups. These metabolites were significantly enriched in metabolic pathways, biosynthesis of secondary metabolites, monoterpenoid and diterpenoid biosynthesis, and phenylpropanoid biosynthesis. In conclusion, resistance of hybrid larch to D. superans is jointly conferred by the defence enzyme system, secondary metabolite accumulation and a 'terpenoid-phenolic' metabolic network: terpenoids and phenolics act synergistically via the terpenoid and phenylpropanoid pathways, together forming the core of chemical defense and supporting the breeding of insect-resistant clones.

papers.title: Mathematical modeling of SUMOylation reveals tissue-specific and dynamic responses to abiotic stress
papers.abstract: SUMOylation is an essential and evolutionarily conserved post-translational modification that enables rapid cellular adaptation to environmental stress. Despite its importance, how the SUMOylation machinery controls its dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated a mathematical model of the plant SUMO cycle with quantitative imaging and biochemical data to decode the regulatory logic of SUMOylation dynamics. The model reveals a fundamental principle: steady-state SUMOylation levels are determined not by the full complement of SUMO-cycle components, but by the abundance of SUMO modifier proteins and E1 enzymes, together with SUMO protease abundance and activity. Strikingly, when we integrated fluorescence measurements from reporters for SUMO-cycle components in Arabidopsis roots after three hours of abiotic stress, the model predicted decreased SUMOylation levels across several tissues, contrary to prevailing evidence. Motivated by this unexpected prediction, we performed time-resolved imaging to better characterize the dynamics of key SUMO-cycle components after salt and osmotic stress. These data revealed highly dynamic component levels within the first three hours of stress that were not captured in the previous measurements. Incorporating this temporal data into the model uncovered a twin-peaked SUMOylation response to salt stress: an early surge underpinned by protease dynamics, followed by a decline and a second peak driven by elevated SUMO modifier and E2 levels. Western blot analysis revealed a corresponding twin-peaked pattern of SUMOylation. Together, our findings demonstrate that the plant SUMO cycle is a highly dynamic system that achieves tissue- and stress-specific control of SUMOylation through the coordinated interplay of multiple SUMO-cycle components.

papers.title: Behavioral dysfunction but not wasting in cancer cachexia is driven by altered tryptophan metabolism
papers.abstract: Cancer cachexia causes pathological weight loss, anorexia, and depressive symptoms, culminating in increased mortality. Using mouse models of pancreatic cancer cachexia, we identify tumor and hepatic inflammatory signaling, multi-organ energy charge depletion, and altered tryptophan metabolism. Metabolomic profiling and stable isotope tracing revealed altered tryptophan fates: serotonin depletion and kynurenine accumulation across tumor, liver, muscle and spleen. Kynurenine accumulation involved accelerated conversion of tryptophan to kynurenine with slowed downstream conversion to kynurenic acid. Restoring serotonin activity pharmacologically or metabolically normalized feeding, locomotion, and depression-like behavior, but wasting, tumor burden, and survival remained unchanged. Blocking kynurenine production or kynurenine-mediated AhR activation pharmacologically produced similar results. Thus, in cancer cachexia, the tryptophan pathway is subverted to deplete serotonin and accumulate kynurenine. This subversion contributes to cachexia-associated behavioral and feeding defects but not lethal systemic catabolism.

papers.title: Multi-Omic and Spatial Profiling Defines Outcome-Associated Tumor States in Head and Neck Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Abstract Head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma (HNACC) shows highly variable clinical behavior that histopathological features only partly predict, and prognostic biomarkers for aggressive disease at diagnosis remain limited. Here, we show by integrating bulk, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomes from 25 HNACC tumors that poor survival is marked by profound loss of myoepithelial tumor cells and expansion of luminal tumor states. Both outcome groups share a myoepithelial-like origin, but aggressive tumors converge on an actively dividing, MYC/E2F-driven luminal state concentrated in discrete spatial niches. Aggressiveness therefore reflects where tumors end along a shared developmental path rather than a distinct lineage or altered immune infiltration. A four-gene classifier capturing this state predicted survival in an independent cohort, outperforming larger signatures and flagging aggressive subgroups in two others. These findings define a lineage proliferation axis linked to HNACC outcome, providing a basis for prospective risk stratification and proliferative-directed therapy.

papers.title: MYC drives endothelial transformation and dedifferentiation in angiosarcoma
papers.abstract: MYC amplification is the most common genetic alteration in radiation-associated angiosarcoma and is also present in a subset of de novo primary angiosarcoma, yet its oncogenic role in this vascular malignancy remains unclear. Here, we report that inducible, endothelial-specific MYC overexpression alone was sufficient to drive angiosarcomagenesis in mice. The resulting pulmonary angiosarcoma tumors exhibited impaired endothelial differentiation, indicative of MYC-driven lineage plasticity. Notably, MYC inactivation in dedifferentiated allografts induced growth arrest and restored endothelial gene expression, demonstrating MYC-dependent reversible cellular plasticity. Integrative analyses of MYC ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq revealed that overexpressed MYC preferentially occupied highly accessible promoters and activated genes involved in cell growth. Consistent with the murine findings, MYC-amplified human angiosarcomas were enriched for MYC target and cell-cycle programs and depleted of endothelial lineage signatures. MYC overexpression in human endothelial and angiosarcoma cells recapitulated these transcriptional changes, enhanced proliferation, and impaired endothelial tube formation. Together, our results establish MYC as an oncoprotein that promotes endothelial lineage plasticity to drive angiosarcoma initiation and progression.

papers.title: Anvaya: phylogenomic analysis of chromosome fusion-and-mixing characters and detection of shared whole-genome duplication
papers.abstract: Chromosome-scale conservation of gene linkage (macrosynteny) provides phylogenetic characters largely independent of sequence data. Fusion of ancestral linkage groups, and especially the subsequent interspersion (mixing) of their genes, is argued to be effectively irreversible, and such synapomorphic events have been used to resolve deep, contentious nodes. I present Anvaya, a dependency-light, open-source toolkit of two Python programs with companion threshold-calibration tools which takes reciprocal-best-hit (RBH) synteny data directly to a phylogenetic analysis that codes fusion and mixing as discrete characters under explicit optimality criteria. The syntenybuilder module builds RBH orthology tables from genome assemblies, using either a designated reference genome or a multi-genome consensus procedure that reconstructs linkage groups de novo, requiring no curated reference set. The character-maps module codes every pairwise linkage-group co-occurrence as unfused, fused-clean or fused-and-mixed from gene order and a Fisher's exact test, then searches for the most parsimonious trees under an unordered (Fitch/Sankoff) and an ordered, irreversible (Camin-Sokal) cost model, optionally under a backbone constraint. Every tree is accompanied by ancestral states, synapomorphies mapped onto clades, consistency and retention indices, bootstrap support, and a permutation test of phylogenetic signal. Anvaya also detects whole-genome and segmental duplication from an intragenomic comparison and recovers the ohnologs that reciprocal best hit structurally drops, which can otherwise render a retained linkage group invisible. Outputs include vector figures and matrices in NEXUS and TNT/Hennig86 formats for verification in PAUP* and TNT. On synthetic data, consensus reconstruction resists a conflicting genome, rescue reverses a total false negative, and the diagnostics flag a deliberately homoplastic character. Across thirteen acarine and outgroup genomes, weakly supported associations concentrate in the most distant genome and in poorly assembled regions. In two duplicated chelicerates, ohnolog rescue recovered 12.5% (Limulus polyphemus) and 2.8% (Mastigoproctus giganteus) and restored three Limulus chromosomes that otherwise carried none.
